paper_title: [PDF] Maintenance Signals in AI-Assisted GitHub Repositories: Evidence from GenAI Adopters
logical_feed_name: impact of GEnAI on OSS Projects

values.study_identification: Empirical repository-mining study of GitHub projects by self-identified GenAI adopters, comparing AI-assisted repositories (identified via agent/MCP configuration files) with matched traditional repositories and analyzing adopter-authored issues to detect maintenance-cost signals (data: May 25–Aug 14, 2025).
values.study_objective: To identify where visible AI assistance appears in adopters’ GitHub projects and what observable maintenance-cost signals emerge, by comparing AI-assisted vs. traditional repositories and classifying issues in AI-assisted repositories.
study_population: 622 GitHub users who publicly signaled GenAI adoption via profile keywords and activity filters.
179 AI-assisted repositories with visible GenAI agent/MCP configuration files.
179 matched traditional repositories from the same adopters (matched by total commits).
248 issues authored by the adopters in AI-assisted repositories.
Initial owner set: 34,204 repositories; 2,004 updated within one month before filtering.
values.genai_definition: GenAI adopters: users whose GitHub profiles contain terms such as “AI Agent”, “AI App”, or “Vibe Coding.” AI-assisted repositories: repositories containing committed (or .gitignore-referenced) configuration files for major GenAI agents or Model Context Protocol (MCP) servers, indicating repository-visible AI assistance.
authors_limitations: Matching based solely on commit counts; potential confounders (domain, team size) not controlled.
Single annotator performed all issue classifications; no inter-rater reliability reported.
Each issue assigned a single outcome label, potentially oversimplifying multi-faceted issues.
GenAI-relatedness and Outcome dimensions are not fully independent; outcome distributions treated as descriptive.
Sampling limited to publicly self-identified, English-keyword adopters; may miss non-disclosing or non-English users and tool-name-only signals; findings not fully generalizable.
Issue activity concentrated in one contributor (163/248); removing this user changes some distributions (UI/UX difference disappears) though External concentration remains significant.
Repository-visible signals capture tools nearer the agent end (e.g., agent/MCP configs); chat-based assistant use leaves no repository trace.
rq1_verification_accountability: Developers still write and review code; verification of generated content remains essential.
External AI service constraints (rate limits, authentication, model availability, output formats) should be documented in READMEs/configs and validated by humans.
Generated/AI-assisted documentation requires human curation, especially for external-resource selection.
rq1_project_size_age: Repositories updated within one month were considered; AI-assisted and traditional repositories were matched by total commit count using the Hungarian algorithm.
rq1_community_structure: Issue creation was highly concentrated: one contributor authored 163/248 issues (65.7%).
rq1_outcome_measure: Mann–Whitney U tests with Bonferroni correction; Cliff’s delta small effects for README length, headers, and code blocks (Table 4).
Traditional repositories show higher URL density per 1k characters (Table 4).
No significant difference in category distributions (Chi-square=5.497, p=0.240; Table 4).
rq1_beneficiary: Project users and contributors (clearer, more structured documentation).
rq1_cost_bearer: Maintainers/developers (verification of generated content; managing external AI dependencies and constraints).
rq1_association_pattern: Visible AI assistance spans all categories; distribution not significantly different from traditional repositories.
rq1_boundary_condition: Categories were auto-classified per Zanartu et al.; repositories were matched only on commit counts; potential misclassification and residual confounding remain.
rq1_supporting_extract: “We found no statistically significant difference in category distribution… (Table 4).”

“AI-assisted repositories had significantly longer README files, with more H1 headers and more code blocks per 1k characters. In contrast, traditional repositories contained more URLs per 1k characters.” (Figure 2; Table 4).
rq2_antecedent: AI-assisted repositories rely on external GenAI provider APIs (e.g., embeddings/model inference) configured via agent/MCP files.
Developers integrate GenAI assistants/agents through repository-visible configuration files.
rq2_intermediate_process: External API calls introduce rate limits, quotas, and dependency/availability management.
AI-specific behaviors require output-format parsing and multimodal decision logic to be maintained.
rq2_mechanism_outcome: Maintenance effort shifts toward managing external dependencies and failures.
Increased need to validate and handle AI-specific outputs and control flow.
rq2_moderator: Provider rate limits and model availability.
Rapid evolution of AI SDKs/protocols (e.g., MCP) affecting compatibility.
rq2_boundary_condition: After removing a dominant contributor, the External concentration for GenAI-related issues remains significant (Fisher’s exact p=0.025; OR 4.16), while the UI/UX difference disappears.
rq2_alternative_explanation: Issue concentration from a single contributor skews UI/UX distribution; repository matching by commits does not control for domain/team size.
rq2_supporting_extract: “GenAI-related issues show a higher proportion of External at 36.3%… [Non-GenAI] predominantly focus on UI/UX at 45.8%.” (Figure 3).
“GenAI-related External issues primarily involve GenAI API failures, such as rate-limit errors…” (Section 3.2; Table 5 examples).
“Removing their issues… GenAI-related issues remain more External… p=0.025, odds ratio 4.16.” (Section 5).
